prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength brought the measurement of time to a fractional uncertainty near 10^-18

statement.case_for: I keep B057 as my single-part position, with Katori and Ye. Having read all eight round-1 statements and my own chair summary, the choice is between a measured, reproduced advance and a younger platform, and I weigh these by the test I always apply to an instrument result: has the claimed performance been reproduced independently, and was the credited idea decisive? For lattice clocks the answer to both is yes. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the trap light shift and lets many atoms be interrogated at once; Ye's group showed what that buys in stability, accuracy and controlled many-body effects. Uncertainty near 1e-18 is reproduced and intercompared across laboratories in Japan, the US, France, Germany and elsewhere, and the clocks are already used for centimetre-scale relativistic geodesy and for limits on varying constants and ultralight dark matter. Both clock-experienced members, Lindroth and Kroll, reach the same conclusion from their own expertise, and every one of the eight opening proposals named the identical pair. That cleanliness of credit is not merit in itself, but it removes the attribution dispute that burdens B015 and B053. I would frame the citation around the lattice clock as a measurement instrument, so it does not reach back into the comb (2005) or ion-control (2012) territory, and does not make the unfinished redefinition of the second part of the discovery.
statement.case_against: The strongest case against is that the lattice clock may be read as a refinement of the optical-metrology line honoured in 2005 and 2012, and that Lemonde, Gill, Hollberg, Ludlow, Takamoto and others made contributions that a two-name citation leaves out. I think these contributions are real but follow-on to the magic-wavelength concept and its high-performance realisation, but I accept this is a judgment and not a proven fact. A second weakness is that B057 is a measurement-science prize and does not speak to the field-opening novelty that three colleagues value in B015; if the committee puts that novelty above attribution cleanliness and demonstrated reproducibility, B015 is a defensible choice, and the citation must then avoid claiming a settled pairing mechanism. I do not support B053 as the lead because no two members propose the same trio, and I do not support a two-part prize, because a three-person limit would force B015 to lose two of its three names while B057 loses none, and the result would be weaker than either part alone.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B015 for its simple, analysable mechanism tied to a decisive experiment, and questions B057 on discovery content, overlap with 2005 and timing relative to the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I accept that the Bistritzer-MacDonald chain is a strong, clean piece of physics, and your argument is the best case for B015; I have moved closer to treating it as the main alternative. But on timing I still disagree. The redefinition of the second is a metrological-body decision that follows from the clocks, and the citation can say so, so the prize does not depend on it. On discovery content, a clock is a measurement, but a measurement whose gain of three orders of magnitude comes from one specific idea, the magic-wavelength lattice, and has been reproduced widely. In B015 the pairing mechanism is open after eight years. I weigh settled and reproduced more heavily at this stage, though I recognise this is where our judgments differ.

responses.point: Olsson argues that B015 is the original experiment, a door opened by a tunable platform, with the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction confirmed in 2018, while conceding that the field is eight years old and the attribution is exposed to Yuan Cao and the Dean group.
responses.response: I agree that the Jarillo-Herrero experiment was the original one and that the platform is real. Your own concession is what decides it for me: you name Yuan Cao and the Dean group as outside the three names, and you describe the field as eight years old with a mechanism still debated. If the committee goes with B015, I would want the citation to be built on flat bands and correlated insulating states, and you should expect the attribution question to be raised. For B057 there is no equivalent exposure to the experiment's lead investigators, because Ye's group is itself the leading experimental source of the performance record.

responses.point: Eriksson sees B015 as a clean case of prediction and experiment closing the loop, with reproduction by many groups across twisted graphene and TMD systems, and asks whether B057's eight-member support should outweigh attribution cleanliness against novelty.
responses.response: The loop-closing argument is strong, and the reproduction across graphene and TMD moire systems is a better maturity case than I first allowed. We differ on where to draw the line: you accept eight years of reproduction as sufficient, and I would accept it for the existence of the phases but not for the pairing mechanism. Your point that the committee should weigh breadth of support against novelty is fair, but I do not treat support counts as a substitute for scientific judgment, and I base B057 on the reproduced 1e-18 record and the credit. I am not asking you to defer to counts, and I keep B015 as my first alternative, so I would not oppose it if the committee prefers it.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B053 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as a theory-then-experiment chain with two decades of reproduction, but concedes that attribution is the real weakness and that B015 or B054 would be cleaner if the credit cannot be settled.
responses.response: I have no scientific objection to topological insulators and I understand why you call the theory-then-experiment chain mature. Your own admission is that the credit cannot be settled in three names: Hasan's 3D branch, and Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang's HgTe proposal, fall outside Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, and Eriksson and Olsson would cut Mele instead. I cannot judge the condensed-matter history, and I rely on you and Mehlig for it, but a prize whose laureate set the committee itself cannot agree on is a weaker basis than one with a shared pair. I keep B053 as my second alternative and would support it if the committee found a trio it could defend.

responses.point: Johansson moved from circuit QED to B057 after reading the ballots, treating the lattice clock as a discovery-and-measurement result with a robust reproduction record, while noting the 2005 and 2012 overlap and the waiting argument.
responses.response: I agree with your reading and with your caution on the overlap. The 2005 prize recognised the comb as a frequency ruler and the 2012 prize recognised control of single quantum systems, whereas the lattice clock's contribution is the many-atom, light-shift-free interrogation that delivered 1e-18. I would write the citation so this distinction is explicit. On Lemonde, Gill and Hollberg I would put the question to the committee openly, but I do not find that they displace the Katori and Ye pair.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads the lattice clock as a distinct achievement or as a refinement of the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether Lemonde, Gill, Hollberg, Ludlow or Takamoto have a claim that a two-name citation cannot honestly omit.

Whether B015's unresolved pairing mechanism, the Yuan Cao and Dean group credit, and the priority of Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto are weaker or stronger obstacles than I can judge as a non-specialist in condensed matter.
Whether waiting for the redefinition of the second would strengthen or weaken the B057 case; I think it is a consequence and not a condition of the discovery.
Whether the committee can find a defensible three-name set for B053, which I cannot judge on its attribution history.
statement.conflict_note: I am Chair, so I take no role in the vote beyond my own ballot. My field is astroparticle physics and detector technology, adjacent to B054 but I have no tie to IceCube (my collaborations are PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur), and I have no tie to Katori, Ye or the B015 and B053 candidates. I note Kroll's disclosed connection to the JILA environment through his year in John Hall's laboratory and the chair summary records it for B057; I treat it as a disclosed proximity, not a recusal. No recusal is needed for me.
